name: Carsten & Mwangi Lakefront Duster
description:
A full-length waxed canvas duster that hits just above the ankle, cut generously through the shoulders to layer over anything. The wax finish is a deep tobacco brown that darkens further when wet, and the collar is wide enough to turn up against a Lake Michigan gale. Double-breasted closure with heavy brass snaps, a rear vent split to mid-thigh for movement, and deep interior pockets sewn from the same canvas. It smells faintly of linseed oil and city rain.

Carsten & Mwangi has been manufacturing outerwear in the Milwaukee corridor for three generations — a family operation that never sold to a corponation and built its reputation entirely on lakefront workers who needed something that would last. This duster is their flagship. It has no tech, no fibers that need charging, nothing that can break. It just works, year after year, until the wax needs reapplying.
what_it_says: You value durability over style and have probably owned this coat for years. You work near the water or grew up doing so.
worn_by: anyone who respects gear that doesn't quit
story_hooks: The coat belonged to someone who disappeared three months ago — their family wants to know why it ended up in a Shelf pawn stall
Carsten & Mwangi just got a hostile acquisition offer from Veldtmann Industries; the family is quietly asking loyal customers for help
A specific batch of these dusters was used to smuggle bioware components sewn into the lining — and someone is tracking down every coat from that run

physical_description.visual_profile: A commanding full-length duster with a relaxed, almost historical silhouette—generous through the shoulders and chest, tapering slightly at the hem which falls just above the ankles. The wide collar frames the face dramatically when turned up. Projects understated durability and lakefront authenticity rather than chrome or augmentation.
physical_description.fit: Deliberately oversized through the shoulders and torso to layer over thermal wear, combat gear, or augmentation harnesses. Straight through the body with minimal taper. The rear vent split to mid-thigh allows unhindered movement for active work. Relaxed but purposeful, not fashion-forward.
physical_description.primary_material: Waxed canvas—heavyweight, tightly woven natural fiber treated with linseed oil-based wax coating. Breathable enough for all-day wear, water-resistant without being synthetic.
physical_description.texture: Smooth waxy surface with subtle canvas weave visible up close. Rich, tactile quality. Darkens noticeably when wet, with beading water across the surface. Develops a subtle patina and creasing over time; the wax deepens in color-stressed areas.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep tobacco brown—warm, earthy, slightly desaturated. Develops darker streaks where moisture accumulates or in high-wear zones (collar, hem, cuffs). No pattern; pure utilitarian monochrome.
physical_description.closures: Double-breasted layout with six heavy brass snaps running down the front. Snaps are large, tactile, and worn—some show greenish patina from lakeside salt air and humidity.
distinctive_features: Wide, substantial collar that turns up fully to cover the neck and jaw against wind
Rear vent split to mid-thigh—practical, historical, allows stride without restricting the garment
Deep interior pockets cut from the same waxed canvas, reinforced at stress points
Brass snaps throughout—no zippers, no tech, no points of electronic failure
Faint linseed oil scent that mingles with urban ozone and lake air
Subtle wear patterns emerging on cuffs and collar from repeated use
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4 functional. Not corpo luxury, not sub-grade salvage. This is the garment of skilled laborers, dockworkers, maintenance crews, and independent operators who value longevity over status. Affordable for working class, respected across all tiers as genuine craft.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing this says: I work for a living, often outdoors, often in harsh conditions. I value durability and function over augmentation and trend. I trust the lakefront tradition. Signals Milwaukee independence, rejection of corpo standardization, respect for craft. Often worn by port workers, transit operators, environmental monitors, and off-grid operators.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and weathered. Rarely pristine. Wax shows darkening at stress points, slight creasing at the elbows and collar. May have visible wear on the cuffs. Smells of linseed oil, city rain, and honest use. The patina is the point.
